title: Clustering Papers by Meaning
answer: Clustering papers by meaning groups research works by what they say rather than by what they cite or which keywords they share. In citation mapping and discovery, it sits beside citation graph analysis and keyword search, giving a semantic view of a literature. For a library of 135 research papers, it can surface themes, near duplicates, and isolated work that citation links alone might miss. The goal is a map of ideas that helps a reader move from one paper to related papers by content.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Clustering papers by meaning groups research works by what they say rather than by what they cite or which keywords they share. In citation mapping and discovery, it sits beside citation graph analysis and keyword search, giving a semantic view of a literature. For a library of 135 research papers, it can surface themes, near duplicates, and isolated work that citation links alone might miss. The goal is a map of ideas that helps a reader move from one paper to related papers by content.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on text embeddings, vector storage, and modest compute. Papers are parsed into clean text, often from abstracts, full texts, or extracted claims, and each passage is turned into a numeric vector by a sentence embedding model. Those vectors live in a vector index or a simple matrix, and clustering runs on a CPU or a single GPU depending on scale. The same pipeline can cover the 12,646 claims extracted from research works, which allows claim level grouping as well as paper level grouping.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical workflow starts with collecting titles, abstracts, and full texts, then cleaning and splitting them into passages. An embedding model converts each passage into a vector, and cosine similarity measures how close two passages are in meaning. Clustering algorithms such as k means, HDBSCAN, or hierarchical clustering then group the vectors, sometimes after a step like UMAP reduces dimensions for visualization. The resulting clusters are labeled by inspecting representative papers or by using topic terms, and the labels are checked against the citation graph to separate genuine thematic groups from artifacts. The output is a set of semantic clusters that can be browsed, searched, and linked back to the original papers.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk begin with the source texts, because abstracts, full texts, and extracted claims carry different licenses and permissions. A responsible pipeline records where each text came from, which model and parameters produced the embeddings, and when the clustering was run, so results can be reproduced or audited. Embeddings can encode biases from training data, and clusters can look objective while hiding arbitrary choices about distance, algorithm, and number of groups. Provenance should also include clear attribution, with links to the original paper rather than to a search tool, and a note that clusters are aids to discovery, not judgments about quality or novelty.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward richer and more dynamic maps. Multilingual embeddings can bring non English papers into the same semantic space, and multimodal models can cluster figures, tables, and text together. Interactive interfaces may let a reader adjust the granularity of clusters, follow a theme over time, or blend semantic similarity with citation paths. Evaluation will matter more as these maps grow, with benchmarks for cluster stability, label quality, and coverage across a library. The likely result is a discovery layer that complements citation mapping rather than replacing it.
